passage:
PASSAGE 1

A. The town of Marlow Bridge, a simulated coastal community of about 18,000 people, decided in 2023 to replace its ageing sea wall. The old wall, built in 1958, had protected the harbour for more than sixty years, but engineers reported that several sections had cracked and that the wall no longer met modern safety standards. The council approved a budget of 4.2 million pounds and appointed a project team led by Dr Helen Marsh, a civil engineer with twenty years of experience in coastal defence. The team was asked to produce a plan within nine months and to consult residents before any construction began.

B. The first stage of the project was evidence collection. Between January and April 2024, the team measured wave heights, recorded tide levels and photographed every metre of the existing wall. They also interviewed 240 residents, shop owners and fishermen. One fisherman, Mr Chen, told the team that the harbour entrance had become shallower over the past decade and that small boats now had to wait for high tide to enter. This information was important because it suggested that the new wall should not simply copy the old design. Dr Marsh noted in her report that 'the sea is not the same sea our grandparents knew' and that any plan based on 1958 conditions would be inadequate.

C. The team then compared three designs. Design A was a taller concrete wall, which would cost 3.8 million pounds and take fourteen months to build. Design B was a sloping rock wall, which would cost 4.6 million pounds and take twenty months. Design C combined a lower concrete wall with a restored salt marsh in front of it; this would cost 4.1 million pounds and take eighteen months. The salt marsh, the team argued, would absorb wave energy and provide a habitat for birds. However, Design C required the council to buy an additional strip of land from two private owners, and negotiations had not yet been completed.

D. Public consultation produced divided opinions. Shop owners near the harbour supported Design A because they wanted construction finished before the summer tourist season. Environmental groups supported Design C, arguing that it offered long-term protection and ecological benefits. Some residents worried that the salt marsh would attract insects and reduce the space available for parking. A retired teacher, Mrs Patel, wrote to the local newspaper saying that the council should 'spend the money on what works, not on what looks pretty'. Dr Marsh responded that the team would publish all measurements and cost estimates online so that residents could examine the evidence themselves.

E. In June 2024, the council voted. Design C received eleven votes, Design A received seven, and two councillors abstained. The council also agreed to fund an independent review of the land purchase. Construction was scheduled to begin in March 2025 and to finish by September 2026. Dr Marsh warned that the timetable depended on the land negotiations and on weather conditions. She also recommended that the town continue to record tide levels every month, because the evidence collected during the project would be valuable for future decisions.

F. Not everyone was satisfied. Mr Chen said he was pleased that the harbour would be improved but disappointed that the fishing community had not been given a permanent seat on the project committee. The council promised to review committee membership in 2027. Meanwhile, the project team began preparing a public exhibition, including photographs of the old wall, maps of the proposed salt marsh and a simple explanation of how the design would reduce wave energy. The exhibition was intended to show residents that the decision had been based on evidence rather than on opinion alone.

PASSAGE 2

A. Memory is not a video recording. Psychologists have shown that when people remember an event, they reconstruct it from fragments, expectations and later information. This process is usually efficient, but it can produce confident errors. In one simulated classroom study, students watched a short film of a bicycle accident and were later asked questions about it. Those who were asked 'How fast was the car going when it passed the bicycle?' estimated higher speeds than those asked 'How fast was the car going when it hit the bicycle?' The change of a single word influenced what participants reported, even though they had all seen the same film.

B. Such findings matter in courts, hospitals and workplaces, where decisions often depend on witness statements. A witness may be honest and still mistaken. For this reason, many organisations now use structured interviews. Instead of asking 'Was the driver wearing a red jacket?', an interviewer might ask 'What can you remember about the driver's clothing?' Open questions reduce the risk that the interviewer's words will shape the answer. Interviewers are also trained to avoid repeating the same question, because repetition can make a witness doubt a correct memory or become more confident about an incorrect one.

C. Confidence is a poor guide to accuracy. In several experiments, participants who were highly confident about a detail were sometimes wrong, while participants who were less confident were sometimes right. Researchers therefore distinguish between the content of a memory and a person's belief about that memory. A witness can say 'I think the car was blue, but I am not certain' and still provide useful information. A statement that includes uncertainty is not necessarily weaker evidence; it may be more honest and more reliable.

D. Digital evidence has changed the picture. Cameras, phones and payment records can provide precise times and locations. However, digital records are not automatically trustworthy. A photograph can be edited, a clock can be wrong, and a message can be sent by someone using another person's account. Investigators therefore check whether digital evidence is consistent with other sources. If a phone record places a person in one street at 8:15 and a witness places the same person in another street at 8:20, the investigator must consider whether the witness's memory of the time is accurate.

E. Organisations can take practical steps. First, record evidence as soon as possible, because memory fades quickly. Second, separate the collection of evidence from the interpretation of evidence; the person who interviews a witness should not also decide what the interview proves. Third, keep a written log of what was collected, when and by whom. Fourth, review decisions when new evidence appears. These steps do not guarantee correct conclusions, but they make errors easier to detect.

F. The study of memory also has implications for education. Students who test themselves regularly remember more than students who simply reread notes. The act of trying to recall information strengthens memory, even when the first attempt is imperfect. Teachers can therefore use short quizzes not only to measure learning but also to improve it. The key is to treat errors as information about what needs to be reviewed, rather than as a final judgement of ability.

PASSAGE 3

A. Urban planners increasingly speak of the 'fifteen-minute city', a model in which residents can reach most daily services within a fifteen-minute walk or cycle ride. The idea is not new; many older neighbourhoods were built before cars became common and already contain shops, schools and clinics within a short distance. What is new is the attempt to measure accessibility systematically and to use the measurements in public decisions.

B. Measuring accessibility requires choices. A planner must decide which services count, how far is 'close enough', and whether to measure distance, travel time or cost. A supermarket may be 500 metres away but separated from a neighbourhood by a busy road with no crossing. In that case, the distance is short but the accessibility is poor. For this reason, some planners use a 'walkability score' that includes pavement width, crossing points, street lighting and traffic speed. A simple map of distances can therefore mislead.

C. Critics raise several concerns. First, the model may suit wealthy city centres better than suburbs or rural areas, where services are naturally more spread out. Second, improving one neighbourhood can raise rents and push lower-income residents elsewhere, a process sometimes called green gentrification. Third, focusing on walking distance may neglect people with disabilities, older residents and those who need to carry heavy shopping. A fifteen-minute city that works only for healthy adults is not a fifteen-minute city for everyone.

D. Supporters respond that the model is a direction, not a fixed rule. They argue that the aim is to reduce unnecessary car journeys and to make streets safer, not to force everyone to walk. They also point out that accessibility can be improved without building new shops: a frequent bus service, a safe crossing or a covered bicycle park can make existing services easier to reach. In one simulated project in the town of Riverton, planners added two pedestrian crossings and a small bus stop; the measured walking time to the nearest clinic fell from twenty-two minutes to fourteen minutes without any new building.

E. Evidence collection is central to the model. Planners in Riverton surveyed 600 residents, recorded journey times at different hours, and mapped the locations of services. They found that the average resident could reach a pharmacy in nine minutes but a hospital in thirty-five minutes. They also found that residents without cars relied heavily on two bus routes, and that these routes stopped running after 7 p.m. This evidence led the council to fund an evening bus service rather than to build a new health centre, because the bus service addressed a more immediate problem at lower cost.

F. The fifteen-minute city is therefore best understood as a method for asking better questions: Who can reach which services, how, and at what cost? The answers will differ from place to place. A model that ignores local evidence may produce attractive maps but poor decisions. A model that uses local evidence carefully can help communities identify the smallest changes that make the largest difference.

SECTION 1: SOCIAL DIALOGUE

You will hear a conversation between a student, Anna, and her friend, Ben, about a volunteering event.

Anna: Ben, have you got a minute? I'm trying to organise the volunteering day for the community centre, and I need a second opinion.
Ben: Sure. What's the problem?
Anna: Well, it's not exactly a problem. We've got three possible dates, and I can't decide which one to choose. The first is Saturday the 12th of April.
Ben: The 12th? That's the same weekend as the town football final, isn't it?
Anna: Is it? I didn't know that. That might be a problem, because a lot of the volunteers are football fans.
Ben: Actually, wait. I think the final is on the 13th, not the 12th. Let me check... yes, the 13th. So the 12th should be fine.
Anna: Good. The second date is Saturday the 19th of April.
Ben: That's the start of the school holidays. Some people will be away.
Anna: That's what I thought. And the third is Saturday the 26th.
Ben: The 26th is after the holidays, so people should be back. But isn't that the day of the library book sale?
Anna: The book sale is on the 25th, I think. Let me look at the notice... yes, the 25th. So the 26th is free.
Ben: Then I'd choose the 26th. It gives people time to come back from holiday, and it doesn't clash with the football or the book sale.
Anna: That makes sense. Now, the second thing: we need to decide what the volunteers will actually do. Last year we painted the hall, but this year the hall has already been painted.
Ben: What about the garden? The back garden is in a terrible state.
Anna: True. But we'd need tools, and we'd need someone who knows about plants.
Ben: My neighbour is a gardener. She might help. But she's away until the 20th.
Anna: That's fine if we choose the 26th. Could you ask her?
Ben: Yes, I'll ask her tomorrow. What else needs doing?
Anna: The kitchen needs cleaning, and the notice board needs repairing. The notice board is probably a one-person job.
Ben: I can do the notice board. I'm not very good at cleaning kitchens.
Anna: Perfect. So we'll do the garden, the kitchen and the notice board. How many volunteers do we need?
Ben: For the garden, maybe six. For the kitchen, three. And one for the notice board. So ten in total.
Anna: Last year we had fourteen, so ten should be manageable. I'll put a sign-up sheet in the hall.
Ben: Good idea. And I'll ask my neighbour about the garden tools.
Anna: Thanks, Ben. You've been a great help.

SECTION 2: SOCIAL MONOLOGUE

You will hear a talk given by a museum volunteer, Claire, to a group of new visitors.

Claire: Good morning, everyone, and welcome to the Marlow Bridge Museum. My name is Claire, and I'm one of the volunteers here. Before you start looking around, I'd like to give you a short introduction to the museum and to explain a few practical things.

The museum opened in 1987, in a building that was originally a school. The school closed in 1975, and for a few years the building was empty. Then a group of local people raised money to turn it into a museum. We now have about 4,000 objects, although only about 800 are on display at any one time. The rest are kept in storage.

The museum is arranged over two floors. On the ground floor, you'll find the local history gallery, which covers the period from 1800 to 1950. This includes tools, clothes, photographs and a reconstruction of a fisherman's kitchen. On the first floor, we have the temporary exhibition space. At the moment, the exhibition is about the sea wall, which some of you may have read about in the newspaper. It includes photographs of the old wall and maps of the proposed new design.

A few practical points. The museum is free to enter, but we welcome donations. There are donation boxes near the entrance and in the first-floor gallery. The café is on the ground floor, next to the shop. It serves hot drinks, sandwiches and cakes, and it closes at 4:30, half an hour before the museum closes. The toilets are on both floors. There is a lift near the main stairs, and it is available for anyone who needs it.

Photography is allowed, but please do not use a flash in the galleries, because the light can damage some of the objects. If you are visiting with children, there is a small activity area on the first floor with books and drawing materials. We also run a free guided tour at 11 o'clock every morning, which lasts about 45 minutes. You don't need to book; just meet at the entrance.

Finally, I should mention that the museum is run almost entirely by volunteers. If you are interested in helping, even for a few hours a month, please speak to me or pick up a leaflet at the desk. We need people to help in the shop, to welcome visitors and to help with school groups. No experience is necessary, and we provide training.

Thank you, and I hope you enjoy your visit.

SECTION 3: ACADEMIC DISCUSSION

You will hear a discussion between two students, Maria and Tom, and their tutor, Dr Lewis, about a research project on memory and evidence.

Dr Lewis: So, Maria, Tom, you've been working on your project about memory and evidence. How is it going?
Maria: Quite well, I think. We've collected most of our data, but we're having some trouble interpreting it.
Dr Lewis: Tell me more.
Maria: Well, we interviewed twenty people about a short film they had watched. We asked half of them one set of questions and half another set. We expected the two groups to give similar answers, but they didn't.
Tom: The group that was asked about the speed of the car gave much higher estimates than the other group.
Dr Lewis: That's interesting. Why do you think that happened?
Maria: At first I thought it was because the two groups were different in some way. But then I checked, and they were similar in age and background.
Tom: So we think the wording of the question affected their answers.
Dr Lewis: That's a reasonable interpretation. But before you conclude that, what else should you consider?
Maria: We should consider whether the film was clear enough. If the film was blurry, people might have guessed.
Dr Lewis: Good. And what about the order of the questions?
Tom: We didn't think about that. We asked the speed question first in both groups.
Dr Lewis: So the order was the same. That's helpful, because it means the difference is less likely to be due to order. But you should still mention it as a limitation.
Maria: We will. We're also worried about the sample size. Twenty people is quite small.
Dr Lewis: Yes, it is. You can't generalise from twenty people. But for a student project, it's acceptable if you are honest about the limitations. What are you planning to do next?
Tom: We're going to write up the results and then compare them with the published studies we read.
Dr Lewis: Good. And remember to separate what you observed from what you think it means. Your observations are the answers people gave; your interpretation is that the wording affected them. Keep those two things distinct in your report.
Maria: That's helpful. We were also thinking of adding a question about confidence, asking people how sure they were.
Dr Lewis: That's a good idea. It might show whether confidence and accuracy are related. But don't be surprised if they are not strongly related. Many studies find that confidence is a poor guide.
Tom: We'll add it. Thank you, Dr Lewis.

SECTION 4: ACADEMIC LECTURE

You will hear part of a lecture on urban accessibility and the fifteen-minute city.

Lecturer: Good afternoon. Today I want to discuss the idea of the fifteen-minute city, and in particular the role of evidence in making it work.

The fifteen-minute city is a model in which residents can reach most daily services within a fifteen-minute walk or cycle ride. The idea has become popular in recent years, but it is not entirely new. Many older neighbourhoods were built before cars became common, and they already contain shops, schools and clinics within a short distance. What is new is the attempt to measure accessibility systematically.

Now, measuring accessibility is not as simple as it sounds. You have to decide which services count. Does a fifteen-minute city need a hospital, or is a clinic enough? You also have to decide what 'close enough' means. Is it distance, travel time or cost? And you have to consider the quality of the route. A supermarket may be only 500 metres away, but if a busy road with no crossing separates it from a neighbourhood, the distance is short but the accessibility is poor.

For this reason, some planners use a walkability score. This score includes pavement width, crossing points, street lighting and traffic speed. A simple map of distances can therefore mislead, because it ignores these factors.

Critics of the model raise several concerns. First, the model may suit wealthy city centres better than suburbs or rural areas, where services are naturally more spread out. Second, improving one neighbourhood can raise rents and push lower-income residents elsewhere. This process is sometimes called green gentrification. Third, focusing on walking distance may neglect people with disabilities, older residents and those who need to carry heavy shopping. A fifteen-minute city that works only for healthy adults is not a fifteen-minute city for everyone.

Supporters respond that the model is a direction, not a fixed rule. The aim is to reduce unnecessary car journeys and to make streets safer, not to force everyone to walk. They also point out that accessibility can be improved without building new shops. A frequent bus service, a safe crossing or a covered bicycle park can make existing services easier to reach.

Let me give you an example from a simulated project in the town of Riverton. Planners there added two pedestrian crossings and a small bus stop. The measured walking time to the nearest clinic fell from twenty-two minutes to fourteen minutes, without any new building. They also surveyed 600 residents and recorded journey times at different hours. They found that the average resident could reach a pharmacy in nine minutes but a hospital in thirty-five minutes. They found that residents without cars relied heavily on two bus routes, and that these routes stopped running after 7 p.m. This evidence led the council to fund an evening bus service rather than to build a new health centre, because the bus service addressed a more immediate problem at lower cost.

So the fifteen-minute city is best understood as a method for asking better questions: Who can reach which services, how, and at what cost? The answers will differ from place to place. A model that ignores local evidence may produce attractive maps but poor decisions. A model that uses local evidence carefully can help communities identify the smallest changes that make the largest difference.

In the next lecture, we will look at how to design a survey and how to avoid common errors in collecting evidence. Thank you.

grammar.title: 高频错误复查：影响理解与作答的句子结构
grammar.explanation: 本周围绕已发现的高频错误做复查，重点不是增加新语法，而是减少影响理解和作答的错误。第一，注意主谓一致和单复数：evidence 是不可数名词，不能说 evidences；data 在学术语境中常作复数，但也可作不可数。第二，注意比较结构：higher than、less likely to be due to 等结构要完整。第三，注意定语从句和分词结构：the group that was asked... 中 that 不能省略到影响理解。第四，注意否定和转折：not... but...、rather than 要看清哪一部分被肯定。第五，注意时间与数字：twelve 和 twenty、fifteen 和 fifty 要区分清楚。
